orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, carrying straight on from Chapter XI. After the quarrel, Catherine has shut herself in her room and refuses to eat, Edgar keeps to the library, and Isabella mopes. It is the middle of winter; scholars date these days to January 1784.

notes.g: The private grounds of the Grange.
notes.m: Not a public park: the open land and trees around a country house.

notes.t: wearying, I guessed, with a continual vague expectation
notes.g: Wearing himself out, I supposed, with constantly half-hoping.
Throw himself down before her, begging forgiveness.
One person with any common sense.
Didn't waste any sympathy on Isabella.
Protests; attempts to reason her out of it.
Come round in their own time.

notes.t: a faint dawn of its progress
notes.g: The first faint signs of things improving.
A water jug and a glass bottle for drinks.
notes.n: A bedroom would have a jug and basin for washing and water for drinking.

notes.g: A bowl of thin, runny porridge, given to sick people.

notes.t: I set down as a speech meant for Edgar’s ears
notes.g: I took to be words meant to be passed on to Edgar.

notes.m: 'Ghastly' meant ghostlike and deathly-looking, not just 'very bad'.
'Society' here means companionship, not the community at large.

notes.t: she acted a part of her disorder
notes.g: She was putting on some of her illness.

notes.t: on the brink of the grave

notes.n: Remember the names scratched on the window ledge in Chapter III: Catherine Earnshaw, Catherine Heathcliff, Catherine Linton.

notes.m: 'The country' often meant the local area, not the nation.

notes.g: Completely unconcerned whether I live or die.

notes.t: What in the name of all that feels
notes.g: What in heaven's name: by everything that has feelings.
Calm acceptance of what can't be helped.

notes.n: After her fever in Chapter IX, Kenneth said she must not be crossed.

notes.m: Nothing to do with paying rent: a 'rent' is a tear in cloth.

notes.g: Arranging them; laying them out in rows.

notes.t: her mind had strayed to other associations
notes.g: Her mind had drifted off to other memories.

notes.t: they put pigeons’ feathers in the pillows—no wonder I couldn’t die
notes.g: A folk belief: a person cannot die on a pillow stuffed with pigeon feathers.
notes.n: Country people sometimes took such a pillow away from a dying person to let them go peacefully.

notes.g: From a moor-cock, a male red grouse.
A crested moorland bird, also called the peewit.
notes.n: Lapwings nest on the ground in open country and wheel and cry over intruders.

notes.t: the clouds had touched the swells
notes.g: The clouds had come down onto the rounded hilltops.

notes.t: the old ones dared not come
notes.g: The parent birds were too frightened to return, so the chicks starved.
Is there blood on them (were they shot)?

notes.m: Not walking about: her mind is wandering.

notes.g: The soft, fine feathers stuffed in the pillow.
In local legend, a cave in the crags where fairies lived.
A rocky outcrop on the moors near Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: Probably based on Ponden Kirk, a rocky outcrop on the moors near the Brontës' home at Haworth. The name echoes nearby Penistone Hill.

notes.g: Ancient flint arrowheads, believed to be fairy weapons.
notes.n: Country people found these prehistoric arrowheads in fields and thought fairies shot them at cattle to make them sicken.

notes.g: Young cows that haven't yet had a calf.
A tall dark wooden cupboard for clothes or linen.
notes.n: Lockwood noticed a 'clothes-press' in the little room at Wuthering Heights where he slept (Chapter III).

notes.g: Gleam like jet, a glossy black stone.
notes.n: Jet was mined at Whitby on the Yorkshire coast and polished for jewellery.
Beds had curtains around them for warmth and privacy.

notes.g: Hung a shawl over the mirror.

notes.m: 'Clothes' here means bedclothes: sheets and blankets.

notes.g: The fir trees outside the window.
notes.n: In Chapter III Lockwood heard a fir branch tapping the window of that very room.

notes.g: Broke her fighting spirit for now.

notes.t: no command of tongue, or brain
notes.g: No control over what I said or thought.
The wooden box-bed with sliding panels in her old room at Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: The same 'oak case' bed Lockwood slept in in Chapter III.

notes.t: the whole last seven years of my life grew a blank
notes.g: She forgot the last seven years entirely.
notes.n: Seven years back takes her to age twelve, just after her father died (end of Chapter V).

notes.g: Old Mr. Earnshaw had just died.
notes.n: His death ends Chapter V. Catherine's diary in Chapter III was written in the days after it.

notes.t: the separation that Hindley had ordered between me and Heathcliff
notes.g: Hindley's new rule keeping the two children apart.
notes.n: After his father's death Hindley pushed Heathcliff down among the servants (Chapter VI).

notes.t: I was laid alone, for the first time
notes.g: I was put to bed alone for the first time.
notes.n: The way she tells it, sleeping alone was part of Hindley's separating her from Heathcliff.

notes.m: 'Late' here means recent, not dead.

notes.g: A sudden violent fit of despair.
The pit of misery I lay in.

notes.t: laughing at injuries, not maddening under them
notes.g: Laughing off hurts instead of being driven mad by them.

notes.n: Heather is the low, purple-flowered shrub that covers the Yorkshire moors.

notes.g: A chill that could kill you.
Not caring about the frosty air.
notes.m: 'Careless of' means heedless of, not sloppy.

notes.g: Go back from the window; go back to bed.
notes.m: 'Retire' here means withdraw, not stop working.

notes.g: The wild strength of someone in a fever.

notes.n: Joseph is the old servant at Wuthering Heights.
'Kirk' is the northern and Scottish word for church. It is the building Nelly also calls the chapel.

notes.g: Faced the ghosts said to haunt it.

notes.m: Not an entrance hall in a hotel: just a corridor outside the rooms.

notes.t: checking the exclamation risen to his lips
notes.g: Cutting off the cry he was about to make.
She is too strong for me.

notes.t: hard to guide any way but her own
notes.g: Hard to manage unless she gets her way.

notes.n: 'Narrow house' or 'narrow home' was an old poetic phrase for the grave.

notes.t: not among the Lintons, mind, under the chapel-roof
notes.g: Not in the Linton family vault inside the church.
notes.n: Wealthy families were often buried inside the church; ordinary people lay outside in the churchyard.

notes.g: Pretend not to see what Heathcliff was up to.
The usual reward for loyalty (sarcastic: blame).

notes.m: 'Intelligence' here means news or information, not cleverness.

notes.t: her wits were alert at applying our conversation
notes.g: Her mind was quick to pick up what we were saying.
Scream out that she takes it all back.
Without waiting to be told; on my own decision.
A metal hook for tying up a horse by its reins.

notes.t: a creature of the other world

notes.g: A springer spaniel, a small lively hunting dog.
notes.n: Her name is Fanny.
He treated Catherine's fever three years earlier (Chapter IX).

notes.t: made no scruple to speak his doubts
notes.g: Didn't hesitate to say he doubted.

notes.n: The first was the fever after Heathcliff vanished (Chapter IX).

notes.g: Strange rumours are going round here.

notes.m: 'Stout' meant sturdy and robust, not fat.

notes.t: that sort of people should not either
notes.g: People of her class shouldn't either.
notes.n: Kenneth seems to mean that the Lintons' kind of gentlefolk are less hardy.

notes.t: flew off in the height of it
notes.g: Rushed away at the peak of it.
Things she imagines that aren't real.
Friendly and close with Mr. Heathcliff.
notes.m: 'Intimate' meant close and familiar, with no sexual sense.

notes.t: discharged from the trouble of calling
notes.g: Spared the bother of visiting (a polite way of saying banned).
Bold hopes of winning Miss Linton, above his station.

notes.t: turn a cold shoulder on him

notes.g: Keeps her thoughts and plans to herself.

notes.m: 'Pretty' here is sarcastic.
Not a large farm growing crops: in England a 'plantation' was a stand of planted trees.

notes.t: mount his horse and away with him
notes.g: Get on his horse and ride off with him.

notes.t: coursed up and down snuffing the grass
notes.g: Ran up and down sniffing the grass, like a hound on a scent.

notes.m: 'Arrest' just meant to stop or check, not a police arrest.

notes.t: suffer matters to take their course
notes.m: 'Suffer' here means allow, not feel pain.

notes.g: A face that hid my alarm badly.

notes.n: Doctors called madness 'alienation', which is why mental doctors were once called 'alienists'.

notes.t: the first proclaimant of her flight
notes.g: The first to announce that she had run away.
What must we have next? (What else can go wrong?)
One of the maids at the Grange.
What's wrong with your young lady?

notes.t: Yon’ Heathcliff’s run off wi’ her!
notes.g: That Heathcliff has run off with her!

notes.m: Literally 'not believable', not 'amazing'.

notes.t: a lad that fetches milk here
notes.g: A boy who brings milk to the house from a farm.

notes.t: a horse’s shoe fastened at a blacksmith’s shop
notes.g: A loose horseshoe nailed back on at the forge.
She recognised them both at once.
notes.m: 'Directly' meant immediately.

notes.g: A gold coin worth one pound: a very generous payment.
notes.n: Strictly, the modern sovereign was first minted in 1817; in 1784 the gold coin would have been a guinea. Brontë uses the coin of her own day.

notes.g: Held the reins of both horses.

notes.t: set their faces from the village

notes.g: Just to go through the motions.
My sister only in name, no longer in feeling.

notes.t: what property she had in the house
notes.g: Whatever belongings she had in the house.
